title: Interfaces
summary: An **interface** describes the *shape* of an object — which properties and methods it must have, and their types. It's TypeScript's primary tool for naming and reusing object contracts across your code.

subtopics.title: Defining an object shape
subtopics.explanation: An interface lists the properties an object must have and their types. Any object assigned to that interface type must satisfy the contract — TypeScript checks at compile time that all required properties are present with the right types.
subtopics.example:
interface User { id: number; name: string; }
const u: User = { id: 1, name: 'Ada' };

subtopics.title: Optional properties
subtopics.explanation: A property suffixed with ? may be present or absent. The type of an optional property includes undefined, so you must handle the missing case before using it. Optional properties are how you model fields that aren't always provided.
subtopics.example: interface User { name: string; nickname?: string; }

subtopics.title: readonly properties
subtopics.explanation: Marking a property readonly means it can be set when the object is created but never reassigned afterward. It's a compile-time guarantee of immutability for that field — useful for ids and configuration that shouldn't change.
subtopics.example: interface Point { readonly x: number; readonly y: number; }

subtopics.title: Method signatures
subtopics.explanation: Interfaces can describe methods, not just data. You declare the method name, its parameter types, and its return type without an implementation. Anything satisfying the interface must provide a matching function.

subtopics.title: Extending interfaces
subtopics.explanation: An interface can extend one or more others, inheriting all their members and adding its own. This builds larger contracts from smaller ones and models 'is-a' relationships between shapes without duplication.
subtopics.example: interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[]; }

subtopics.title: Declaration merging
subtopics.explanation: Declaring the same interface name twice merges the declarations into one — TypeScript combines their members. This is unique to interfaces (types can't do it) and is how you augment existing types, such as adding a property to the global Window.

subtopics.title: Implementing in classes
subtopics.explanation: A class can declare implements SomeInterface, and the compiler then enforces that the class provides every member the interface requires. This is how you guarantee a class conforms to a contract, enabling interchangeable implementations.
subtopics.example: class ConsoleLogger implements Logger { log(m: string) { console.log(m); } }

subtopics.title: When to reach for an interface
subtopics.explanation: Use interfaces for object and class shapes that may be extended, implemented, or merged — they communicate intent well and give clean error messages. For unions, tuples, or mapped/derived types, reach for a type alias instead.
subtopics.example: interface ApiResponse { ok: boolean; data: unknown; }

foundations.overview: Interfaces are TypeScript's way of giving a name to the shape of an object. Instead of repeating a long inline object type, you declare an interface once and reference it everywhere. The compiler then checks every object claiming that type against the contract, catching missing or mistyped properties before the code runs. Interfaces also support inheritance (extends), class conformance (implements), and merging.
foundations.formalDefinition: An interface is a named, purely structural type that describes the members (properties and methods, with their types and modifiers) an object or class must have. TypeScript uses structural typing: any value with a compatible shape satisfies the interface, regardless of how it was declared.
foundations.whyItMatters: Interfaces are the backbone of typed object-oriented and functional TypeScript — they define API contracts, component props, function options, and class abstractions. Clear interfaces make code self-documenting and let the compiler enforce that producers and consumers of data agree on its shape.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an interface as a checklist a contractor must satisfy. The interface lists required rooms (properties) and features (methods); any building (object/class) that has all of them passes inspection, no matter who built it. TypeScript is the inspector checking the list at compile time.
foundations.browserPerspective: Interfaces exist only at compile time and are completely erased — the emitted JavaScript contains no interfaces and no runtime shape checks. They influence what the compiler allows you to write, not what runs in the browser.
foundations.realWorldUsage: React component props (interface Props), API response shapes, function option bags ({ retries?: number }), and class contracts (implements Repository) are all expressed as interfaces in everyday TypeScript code.
foundations.businessImpact: Well-defined interfaces act as enforced contracts between teams and modules, so a change to a data shape surfaces as compile errors at every consumer rather than as runtime bugs in production.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Interfaces enable programming to a contract: code depends on a shape, not a concrete implementation, which makes substitution, mocking in tests, and refactoring safe and mechanical.
foundations.performanceImpact: Zero runtime cost — interfaces are erased. As a bonus, the compiler can often type-check against named interfaces faster and produce clearer error messages than against large inline object types.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Interfaces exist at runtime and validate objects.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Interfaces are erased at compile time; they perform no runtime checks. To validate data at runtime you need an explicit check or a validation library.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An object must be declared as the interface type to satisfy it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: TypeScript is structural — any object with a compatible shape satisfies the interface, regardless of how or where it was created.

config.intro: Trace how interface User { id: number; name: string } is enforced.

steps.name: Declare the interface
steps.detail: interface User { id: number; name: string } names a contract: every User needs a numeric id and a string name.

steps.name: Annotate a variable
steps.detail: const u: User = ... tells the compiler u must satisfy the User shape.

steps.name: Check required members
steps.detail: The compiler verifies id and name are present with the correct types — a missing field is an error.

steps.name: Reject extra/wrong fields
steps.detail: An object literal with a typo'd or mistyped property fails the check at compile time.

steps.name: Extend the contract
steps.detail: interface Admin extends User adds members while inheriting id and name.

steps.name: Erase at compile time
steps.detail: The interface vanishes from the output; only the plain JavaScript object remains at runtime.

debuggingLab.title: A class silently misses an interface member
debuggingLab.symptom: Code calls repo.findById but the implementation only defined find, so the call is undefined at runtime — the interface wasn't actually enforced.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Without 'implements Repository' the compiler never verifies that UserRepo provides findById, and typing the instance as any hides the gap. The method name mismatch (find vs findById) only surfaces at runtime.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the implements clause, so the interface contract isn't enforced.
Typing the instance as any, which suppresses the missing-method error.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add implements Repository and a correct instance type so the compiler enforces the method name.

theory.question: What is an interface in TypeScript and why use one?
theory.directAnswer: An interface names the shape of an object — the properties and methods it must have, with their types. You use it to give a reusable name to a contract, so the compiler can check that every object or class claiming that type actually matches it. Interfaces make code self-documenting, prevent missing-or-mistyped-field bugs, and support extension, implementation, and merging.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A named, structural description of an object's members and their types.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To define and reuse contracts for object shapes and class abstractions instead of repeating inline types.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: TypeScript checks any value annotated with the interface structurally — if its shape is compatible, it satisfies the interface, and the interface is then erased from the compiled output.

theory.whyImportant: Interfaces are the everyday tool for typing props, API shapes, and class contracts, so they're a baseline TypeScript skill interviewers expect.
theory.realWorldExample: A React component's props are typically declared as an interface (interface Props { title: string; onClose: () => void }).

nestedTopics.title: Optional & readonly
nestedTopics.explanation: ? marks a property optional; readonly forbids reassignment after creation.

nestedTopics.title: extends
nestedTopics.explanation: An interface can inherit members from one or more other interfaces.

nestedTopics.title: Structural typing
nestedTopics.explanation: Any compatible shape satisfies the interface, regardless of declaration.

followUps.question: Do interfaces exist at runtime?
followUps.answer: No — they're erased during compilation and perform no runtime validation. The emitted JavaScript has no trace of them.

followUps.question: Can a class implement multiple interfaces?
followUps.answer: Yes — a class can implement several interfaces at once and must satisfy every member of each.

theory.question: What is declaration merging and how does it apply to interfaces?
theory.directAnswer: Declaration merging means declaring the same interface name more than once causes TypeScript to combine all the declarations into a single interface containing the union of their members. It's unique to interfaces — type aliases can't be merged. Its main practical use is augmenting existing types, such as adding a property to a third-party interface or to the global Window object without modifying the original source.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Automatic combination of multiple interface declarations sharing one name.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To allow extending or augmenting types you don't own, including global and library types.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler gathers every interface declaration with the same name and merges their members into one effective interface.

theory.whyImportant: It's a distinguishing feature of interfaces (vs type aliases) and the standard mechanism for module/global augmentation.
theory.realWorldExample: Adding declare global { interface Window { dataLayer: unknown[] } } to type an analytics global.

nestedTopics.title: Global augmentation
nestedTopics.explanation: Merging into Window or other ambient interfaces to add typed globals.

nestedTopics.title: Library augmentation
nestedTopics.explanation: Extending a library's interface to add custom fields it doesn't ship.

followUps.question: Can you merge a type alias the same way?
followUps.answer: No — redeclaring a type alias is a duplicate-identifier error. Only interfaces support declaration merging.

scenario.question: Your team has several services that all need a 'logger'. How do you use interfaces so they're interchangeable and testable?
scenario.directAnswer: Define a Logger interface with the methods you need (e.g., log and error), then have each concrete logger — ConsoleLogger, FileLogger, a NoopLogger for tests — declare implements Logger. Services depend on the Logger interface, not a concrete class, so you can swap implementations freely and inject a fake logger in tests. The compiler guarantees every implementation provides the full contract.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Programming to an interface so multiple implementations are substitutable.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To decouple consumers from concrete classes, enabling substitution and easy mocking.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: implements forces each class to satisfy the interface; consumers accept the interface type, so any implementation fits.

scenario.whyImportant: Depending on contracts rather than concretions is core to testable, maintainable code and a common design discussion in interviews.

nestedTopics.title: Dependency inversion
nestedTopics.explanation: High-level code depends on the interface, not the concrete logger.

nestedTopics.title: Test doubles
nestedTopics.explanation: A NoopLogger or spy implementing Logger swaps in cleanly for tests.

followUps.question: Why an interface here instead of a base class?
followUps.answer: An interface imposes a contract with no implementation or inheritance baggage, so unrelated classes can satisfy it and a class can implement several interfaces at once.

coding.question: Design interfaces for a shopping cart: an Item with name and price, and a Cart with an items array plus an addItem method and a total method. Provide a class implementing Cart.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll start with a small Item interface for the data shape. The Cart interface describes the contract: an items array of Item, an addItem method that takes an Item and returns void, and a total method returning a number. Then a ShoppingCart class declares implements Cart, so the compiler enforces every member exists with the right signature. total just sums the prices.
coding.lineByLine: Item names the element shape. Cart declares the data field items and two method signatures with no bodies. ShoppingCart implements Cart, so the compiler checks it provides items, addItem, and total exactly. addItem pushes onto the array; total reduces the prices. If any member were missing or mistyped, compilation would fail.
coding.timeComplexity: addItem is O(1); total is O(n) over the items.

alternativeApproaches.title: Readonly items via accessor
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Expose items as readonly to prevent external mutation, mutating only through addItem.
alternativeApproaches.code: interface Cart { readonly items: readonly Item[]; addItem(i: Item): void; total(): number; }

followUps.question: Why declare implements Cart on the class?
followUps.answer: It makes the compiler enforce that the class provides every member of the contract; without it, a missing or mistyped method wouldn't be caught until runtime.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Interfaces define the contracts between layers: API DTOs, service abstractions (implements), repository interfaces, and component props. Consumers depend on interfaces rather than concrete implementations, which keeps modules loosely coupled and lets implementations vary without rippling changes through callers.
productionDeepDive.performance: Interfaces are erased and add no runtime overhead. Naming shapes as interfaces (rather than large inline object literals) can also speed up type-checking and produce more readable compiler error messages in big projects.
productionDeepDive.security: Because interfaces are erased and do no runtime validation, never assume external data matches its interface. Validate untrusted input (request bodies, API responses) at runtime and only then treat it as the interface type.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Shared interface definitions act as a single source of truth for shapes across many modules or even a monorepo, so a contract change produces compile errors at every affected site, making large-scale refactors tractable.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Keep interfaces focused and composable via extends rather than building one giant interface. Use declaration merging deliberately and sparingly for augmentation, since silent merges can surprise readers.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI enforces every interface contract before code ships, surfacing missing or mistyped members as build failures rather than runtime errors.

caseStudies.problem: Components and services shared object shapes that drifted out of sync, causing runtime errors.
caseStudies.solution: Centralized shapes as interfaces, typed props and DTOs with them, and used implements for service contracts.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Some upfront design effort vs. compiler-enforced consistency across the whole app.
caseStudies.lessons: Interfaces turn shape agreements into enforced contracts, catching drift at build time instead of in production.

keyTakeaways: An interface names the shape of an object — its required properties and methods with their types.
Use ? for optional properties and readonly for fields that can't be reassigned after creation.
extends composes interfaces; implements forces a class to satisfy a contract; both are checked at compile time.
Declaration merging (redeclaring an interface name) is unique to interfaces and is used to augment existing types.
Interfaces are structural and erased at runtime — they do no validation, so validate untrusted data separately.
